title: No motive except violence: The twin brothers who planned the Victoria bank shootout
subtitle: The pair may have intended to re-enact the 1997 North Hollywood shootout
article: Precisely one week after a quiet Victoria street exploded into a shootout with heavily armed bank robbers, Saanich Police Chief Constable Dean Duthie told a Tuesday press conference it was sheer chance that the city's tactical squad just happened to be nearby.
"I don't want to even think about what could have happened if they had not been there," he said.

Duthie noted that of six officers wounded in the shootout, three remained in hospital, in intensive care. Although the chief constable refused to release the names or even the specific injuries suffered by the officers, he said both were conscious and able to hold conversations.
"The injuries are significant but the recovery process has started," said Duthie. "It is a shocking event that we're still processing."

Among the most shocking developments so far was the revelation over the weekend that the whole thing had been orchestrated by a pair of 22-year-old twin brothers who could very well have been motivated by nothing more than a fetish for violence.

They had no criminal records. But their social media abounded with photos of firearms and armed conflict. And witnesses reported that the brothers acted as if they relished a confrontation with law enforcement.
Shelli Fryer, who was in the bank at the time of the robbery, told CFAX 1070 that after the robbers had been escorted to the bank's vault, they inexplicably waited around until police arrived.
"What were they waiting for?... They could have just taken the money and left right away," she said.
Instead, the two suspects opened fire almost immediately on a white van carrying officers from the Greater Victoria Emergency Response Team, riddling it with bullet holes.

A viral video shot from across the street captured what happened next: Officers sprinting towards the bank and pouring gunfire at the suspects as near-constant shots ring out. The two robbers were killed at the scene. Miraculously, no civilians were injured.

On Saturday, B.C. RCMP confirmed that the two dead robbers were Mathew and Isaac Auchterlonie. Coming from Duncan - roughly an hour north of Victoria - the pair appear to have driven to the bank in a 1992 Toyota Camry with racing stripes on the hood.

While the typical motive for a bank robbery is money, police aren't so sure in this case. "The motive behind the armed robbery and subsequent exchange of gunfire with police has not yet been determined," read a statement by RCMP Cpl. Alex Bérubé.

The Canadian Armed Forces confirmed this week that Matthew had attempted to enlist in the military, but was rejected after failing the Canadian Forces Aptitude Test. The test, several practice versions of which exist online, is a multiple choice test mainly consisting of math and English at a roughly 10th grade level.

Otherwise, most of what is known about the brothers comes by way of an Instagram account maintained by Isaac. In a brief bio, Isaac describes himself as a "patriot" and "WW2 Pacific War enthusiast." The posts are devoted almost entirely to clips from Hollywood war films and war documentaries interspersed with the occasional anti-government meme.
In one video uploaded by the account holder, a hand can be seen taking a pamphlet announcing a Trudeau government ban on "assault-style" firearms and lighting it on fire.

Other uploaded images and video show a selection of long guns being showcased and fired by the brothers, including a Russian SKS semi-automatic and a Mossberg 500 shotgun. Both guns are legal to possess as "non-restricted" firearms in Canada, although the posts show magazines that are illegally modified to hold more than five rounds, which are referred to as "freedom seeds."

Public attention has focused in particular on a post commemorating the anniversary of the 1997 North Hollywood shootout, a California bank robbery that bore striking similarities to the brothers' own attempted heist.

Two perpetrators clad in homemade body armour and carrying heavy weapons robbed a Bank of America branch before engaging in a public shootout with the Los Angeles Police Department that famously highlighted the low power of police weapons at the time; many pistol rounds fired at the robbers simply bounced off harmlessly.

In several local media interviews, retired Saanich officer Chris Horsley has noted the eerie parallels between the 1997 shootout and last week's robbery. "I don't know if this is a copycat... but I think you'll be somewhat shocked at the similarities," he told Victoria radio Adam Stirling.

The 1997 incident would end up being instrumental in compelling U.S. and Canadian law enforcement to equip and train for encounters with heavily armed and armoured suspects. It's this exact doctrine that may have resulted in the Auchterlonies being so swiftly taken down by Victoria police.
Said Duthie on Tuesday, "I know the training is very extensive."
